title: Foundations of Mindfulness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating mindfulness and awareness in daily life through embodied practice, exploring early Buddhist teachings, and developing qualities such as gratitude, motivation, and equanimity. Nomon Tim Burnett highlights the value of physical presence and embodiment in Buddhist practice, noting that it's not just about intellectual understanding but also about direct experience and connection with one's own body. By incorporating mindfulness practices into daily life, individuals can develop a greater sense of purposefulness, stability, and clarity, leading to a more fulfilling and meaningful existence.

sentences.text: Well, before I start talking away using words and concepts, because that's what we've got, I just want to express a little appreciation for how we do this practice with our bodies.
It's not a bunch of ideas, actually, right?
It's felt, it's moved, it has a position, it has weight, mass.
It's a beautiful thing to practice in a body.
I think practice has really helped me be more in my body.
I feel like I have a long way to go, but I feel a lot more in my body and I'm really grateful for that.
I was talking to somebody about being a priest, and I was talking to Seishu and I can tell you that.
They were helping me remember what an embodied thing it is, and that learning to be a practitioner, learning to be a priest, any kind of practitioner, you learn from each other's bodies, actually.
At one point when I was getting to co-teach with Jeff Kelly a lot, when he was the teacher in Seattle, I remember those days if you were here.
I miss that.

I go up and offer incense like Judith.

That's the way we do it.
We have our own way of doing it, but it's my version of Norman's way.
I want to also thank our wonderful and remarkably steady gang of practice leaders who have been giving the talks for a while.

Maybe I forgot, but I think I haven't been in this seat in a while.

Oh, they're great.
Really thoughtful.
People really took that on.
The thing that makes me happiest is the times when our teachers tell us about their own practice.
Don't you think?
That's the best part.
I don't know if you were here for Hannah's story about the post office.
It will now always be a great Dharma story in my heart.
So I'll just leave you that teaser for her talk on right speech if you weren't here.
You can find out about the Bodhisattva who takes care of the Marble Mount Washington post office and how Hannah became that person's student.
As Chris mentioned last week, these teachings, the Eightfold Path, the Four Noble Truths, are from the earliest, or maybe nearly earliest, strata of Buddhism.
There are actually some very early Buddhist teachings that don't mention any of that.
Although the teaching which first introduces them says this is the first teaching, we'll never exactly know who said what when.
It's lost in the midst of history, but certainly early.
And you won't actually find Zen teachings that mention directly, that I'm aware of, right view or right intention or right livelihood.
I don't know of great sayings from the great Zen teachers or koans that mention any of these things directly, but it's always there.
It's always there in the background and in the training of those practitioners.

Part of their training was to more or less memorize the whole, I don't know if they all did this, some of them were just there because there was no food anywhere else, but the ones that really got into it would more or less memorize the entire corpus of Buddhist teachings, the entire Tripitaka, and so this is in there.
They would know it and they would have practiced with it.
But the Zen tradition then got interested in going beyond all teachings and created a whole lot of teachings about going beyond teachings.
So that's more our family style, to feel into what's beyond these teachings, but the only way to know what's beyond is to deeply practice them in their own right.

So I thought for the rest of the year it would be nice to keep exploring, not religiously, the early Buddhism, which is usually looked at in one great collection that was recorded in a South Indian language called Pali.
It's no longer a living language, and it became a kind of church Latin of early Buddhism.
But nothing was written down, as you probably remember, for quite a long time.
We don't even know when the Buddha lived.

Somebody told me once there was an entire week-long academic conference where they argued about that night and day based on textual evidence, because there's actually no archaeological evidence of when the Buddha lived.
But the teachings were written down, memorized and repeated.
Monks and nuns recited them, sometimes in groups, learning them so they could recite them.
Some monks or nuns would specialize in different parts of the text.

I was thinking about that today, and I thought, God, just the other day I was at a meeting in the early afternoon with a few people, and then a couple of hours later one of the members of our little meeting group sent a summary by email, and several things that they put in the summary I did not think were the things that had been said.
This is a couple of hours later.
So how did they keep this going for 500 years, when it was all written down right around the time of Christ?

But on the other hand, they were really taking it seriously in a way that maybe we have lost touch with, really devoting their lives to paying attention, being present and remembering these teachings.

Here are monks and nuns.
